title: Teaching and Identity
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien reflects on teaching as identity and on why work/life balance is so hard for committed teachers. He describes the pull between the teacher who is obsessed with best practice and the parent and runner outside school, and argues that many conflicts over change in schools are really identity conflicts, with teachers resisting pedagogy that threatens their beliefs. He admits to feeling this from the other side as a school leader who knows more effective practice than the school can adopt quickly, and he accepts that incremental progress still counts. On wellbeing he is sceptical of token gestures like early-finish meetings and mandated yoga, noting that teachers carry the mental weight of up to 100 students. His answer is to prioritise the elements of identity that make him whole, from exercise and reading to family routines, while accepting that missing any of them is fine. He ends by citing David Didau on how school culture limits what teachers can sustain.
points: Teaching easily absorbs a whole identity, so work/life balance depends on deliberately protecting the parts of yourself that are not the teacher.
Resistance to change in schools is partly identity protection, because new pedagogy that contradicts a teacher’s beliefs feels like an attack on who they are.
Brien’s own tension is the curse of knowledge, knowing better practice while leading a school that can only change slowly through the carrot rather than the stick.
Workplace wellbeing gestures such as an early-finish meeting or mandated yoga are trivial next to the real mental weight of caring for up to 100 students.
His concrete practices are daily exercise, a nightly novel chapter, family routines and refusing to play school with his daughter, plus the humility to miss any one of them without crisis.
quotes: This creates one of the biggest identity conflicts in teachers when schools implement strategies or pedagogy that conflicts with their internal beliefs. This is one of the biggest causes of resistance to change as individuals push back as a form of self-protection as changing may go against their own ideology and therefore damage the personal belief of their own identity.

Schools are complex organisations which require slow sequential change over time. This means that sometimes this involves allowing less effective practices to continue in the short term as the carrot creates more buy in than the stick.

This work/life balance often gets trivialised in the workplace as statements get made such as “We’re giving you this 10 minutes back” when a staff meeting ends early or email blackout periods which really mean that emails get scheduled to pop into your inbox as soon as they are allowed again. Sometimes, this also appears as a workplace mandated wellbeing activity where for an hour you all must go through a guided meditation or yoga3 session to be ‘mindful’ while you tend to stress about all of the work related tasks you could’ve completed in that hour to free up more of your personal time.

Without a true work/life balance teachers are on a direct ride to burnout as teachers do not just carry the burden of marking and admin tasks. They also carry the mental weight of the wellbeing of anywhere up to or over 100 other human beings.

I think it is mainly about prioritising the elements of your identify that make you feel whole and actively trying to avoid anything that brings you back into your working mindset. For example: my daughter is currently 6. She’s in grade 1 and absolutely loves school. Every single morning she requests that we play schools and for my own mental wellbeing I have to say no. It’s tough to do because I love playing with her but there is nothing I would like to play less when we are together because I do not want to feel like her teacher. I need that separation of Church and state.
Even these can be tricky in terms of creating a healthy balance of identity as to truly have balanced wellbeing one needs to be okay with missing out on any of these things for a day or two

In considering whether a teacher is likely to improve, where they work matters. Teachers are not free-floating units of effectiveness. They are constrained by the schools they work in. The culture of a school affects what teachers can sustain, what they come to see as normal, and whether they are likely to improve over time.
